stages.name: Debt relief: advantages and disadvantages
stages.title: Debt relief: advantages and disadvantages
stages.sub: Weigh up what a country gains and risks when its debt is cancelled or reduced.

steps.q: A developing country's government used to spend a third of its tax revenue just repaying old loans. That debt is now cancelled. What can it do with the money it used to send abroad each year?
steps.right: Spend it on things like schools and hospitals at home
steps.wrong: It has no extra money to spend, since the loan is gone
steps.hint: The repayments stop, but the tax revenue still comes in every year. Where does that money now go?

steps.q: With that freed-up money going into healthcare, education and infrastructure, what is likely to happen to the country's long-run growth and living standards?
steps.wrong: They are unlikely to change at all
steps.hint: More spending on schools, hospitals and roads usually feeds into what over time?

steps.q: A country has its debt cancelled, but its government keeps spending more than it collects in tax and borrows heavily again a few years later. What is the risk of wiping the slate clean like this?
steps.right: The country may build up unsustainable debt again
steps.wrong: The country will be permanently unable to borrow again
steps.hint: Cancelling the debt does not change the government's habit of overspending. What might happen once lenders are willing to lend again?

steps.q: Knowing that badly-run debts might get cancelled in future, how might this affect a government's incentive to borrow and spend responsibly now, and lenders' incentive to check who they lend to?
steps.right: It weakens the incentive to borrow and lend responsibly
steps.wrong: It has no effect on how governments or lenders behave
